description: GPU and CPU cloud services for training and inference, including managed GPU provisioning, cluster scheduling, and cloud-native ML platforms.
parity_rationale: Open source orchestrators (Ray, SkyPilot, Volcano) cover scheduling and multi-cloud provisioning, but managed GPU availability and pricing remain dominated by hyperscalers.

description: Libraries for distributed computing across machines — collective operations, gradient synchronization, and inter-node communication for training at scale.
parity_rationale: NCCL and Gloo are open and widely used, but tightly coupled to NVIDIA hardware. Cross-vendor distributed training remains fragmented.

description: Tools that optimize models for specific hardware — graph compilers, kernel generators, and model conversion pipelines (TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, TVM, Triton).
parity_rationale: Open compilers (TVM, Triton, MLIR) are viable but lag behind vendor-optimized stacks (TensorRT, XLA) in production performance and hardware coverage.

description: Low-level software that interfaces with accelerator hardware — CUDA, ROCm, Metal, and driver-level APIs.
parity_rationale: CUDA dominates with no open equivalent. ROCm is open but AMD-only. Limited direct repo coverage — most firmware is proprietary.

description: AI-specific chips and accelerators — GPUs, TPUs, custom ASICs, and neuromorphic hardware.
parity_rationale: Hardware is inherently proprietary. Open efforts (RISC-V AI extensions, OpenTPU designs) are early-stage. NVIDIA, Google, and custom silicon vendors lead.

description: Core deep learning frameworks — PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow, MLX — providing tensor operations, autograd, and training loops.
parity_rationale: PyTorch and JAX are the dominant training frameworks and both fully open. This is the strongest layer in the open source AI stack.

description: Data storage and retrieval for large-scale ML — data loaders, distributed file systems, vector databases, and dataset management.
parity_rationale: Open tools exist (MinIO, LanceDB, WebDataset) but managed storage and retrieval at scale is dominated by cloud vendor offerings.

description: Scripts, harnesses, and frameworks for benchmarking model performance — HELM, lm-evaluation-harness, EleutherAI eval tools.
parity_rationale: Open eval harnesses are widely used and many closed providers publish results on them. Gap is in proprietary internal eval suites that closed labs use but don't release.

description: Code for adapting pretrained models to specific tasks — PEFT, LoRA, TRL, QLoRA, and fine-tuning frameworks.
parity_rationale: Open fine-tuning tools (PEFT, TRL, Axolotl) are production-grade. Closed labs have internal tooling but the open ecosystem is catching up quickly.

description: Code for running models in production — vLLM, TGI, llama.cpp, and inference engines optimized for latency and throughput.
parity_rationale: vLLM and TGI are best-in-class inference engines used by both open and closed providers. Strong open source position.

description: Neural network structure definitions — attention mechanisms, transformer variants, mixture-of-experts, state-space models.
parity_rationale: Architecture innovation is published in papers but leading labs (Google, OpenAI, Anthropic) keep production architectures proprietary. Open reproductions lag by months.

description: Utility libraries for tokenization, data loading, prompt formatting, and other model-adjacent tooling.
parity_rationale: HuggingFace tokenizers, datasets, and safetensors are the standard. Open source dominates this layer.

description: End-to-end training pipelines and scripts — Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed, Composer, NeMo, and distributed training infrastructure.
parity_rationale: Open training stacks (DeepSpeed, Megatron, NeMo) are used to train frontier-class models. The code is open even when the resulting weights aren't.

description: Standard datasets for measuring model performance — MMLU, HellaSwag, HumanEval, and domain-specific evaluation sets.
parity_rationale: Most major benchmarks are publicly available. Gap is in proprietary internal test sets that closed labs maintain.

description: Tools for cleaning, filtering, deduplicating, and preparing training data — annotation platforms, data pipelines, and quality filters.
parity_rationale: Open tools (Label Studio, Argilla, datatrove) are viable but enterprise-grade data pipelines at scale remain a closed-source strength.

description: Human feedback data for RLHF, DPO, and alignment — preference pairs, reward model training sets, and constitutional AI datasets.
parity_rationale: Open preference datasets (Open Assistant, Nectar, UltraFeedback) are substantial. Closed labs generate proprietary RLHF data but open alternatives are competitive.

description: Large-scale corpora used to train foundation models — Common Crawl, The Pile, RedPajama, FineWeb, and web-scale text datasets.
parity_rationale: Open corpora exist but are smaller and less curated than what closed labs use. Data quality and curation at frontier scale remains a closed advantage.

description: Machine-generated data for training augmentation — distillation outputs, synthetic instruction sets, and data generation pipelines.
parity_rationale: Closed labs generate high-quality synthetic data from their own frontier models. Open tools (distilabel, Cosmopedia) are emerging but lag in quality.

description: Foundation model weights before fine-tuning — Llama, Mistral, Falcon, Gemma, and other base model releases.
parity_rationale: Open base models (Llama 3, Mistral, Qwen) are competitive with closed frontiers on many benchmarks. The gap has narrowed significantly since 2023.

description: Quantized, pruned, or distilled models optimized for efficiency — GGUF, GPTQ, AWQ formats and compressed model variants.
parity_rationale: Open quantization tools are strong (llama.cpp, GPTQ) but closed providers optimize internally with proprietary techniques. Open models often rely on community quantization.

description: Models fine-tuned for specific fields — medical (Med-PaLM), legal, financial, scientific, and code-specialized models.
parity_rationale: Domain models require specialized data that closed providers often have through partnerships. Open domain models exist but coverage is uneven.

description: Instruction-tuned and chat-optimized model weights — Llama Chat, Vicuna, Zephyr, and RLHF-aligned conversational models.
parity_rationale: Closed chat models (GPT-4, Claude) still lead on safety, instruction-following, and user experience. Open chat models are rapidly improving.

description: Models handling multiple modalities — vision-language (LLaVA, GPT-4V), audio-language, video, and cross-modal models.
parity_rationale: Open multimodal models (LLaVA, Whisper, CLIP) are competitive. Video and real-time multimodal remain closed-led.

description: Tools for serving and scaling models in production — containerization, model serving platforms, API gateways, and deployment automation.
parity_rationale: Open deployment tools (BentoML, Seldon, KServe) are production-grade. MLOps deployment is a strong open source area.

description: Frameworks for building AI agents — LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen, and tool-use orchestration libraries.
parity_rationale: Agent frameworks are overwhelmingly open source. The gap is in production reliability and enterprise features, not availability.

description: Controls for structured output — temperature, response format, JSON mode, function calling schemas, and generation constraints.
parity_rationale: Closed APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic) lead in structured output reliability. Open tools (Outlines, Instructor) are catching up but less battle-tested.

description: System-level prompt configuration and management — prompt templates, prompt versioning, and system message tooling.
parity_rationale: Prompt management is fragmented in open source. Closed platforms bundle prompt engineering directly into their APIs.

description: Monitoring, logging, tracing, and debugging for LLM applications — LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix, and OpenTelemetry integrations.
parity_rationale: Open observability tools exist (Langfuse, Phoenix) but closed platforms (LangSmith, Datadog LLM) offer more integrated experiences.

description: User-facing interfaces and API endpoints — chat UIs, playground apps, API wrappers, and developer portals.
parity_rationale: Open chat UIs (Open WebUI, LibreChat) exist but lack the polish and integration of ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini interfaces.

description: Data cards, provenance records, and lineage documentation — Croissant, dataset cards, and data governance tooling.
parity_rationale: Open standards (Croissant, HF dataset cards) exist but adoption is inconsistent. Closed providers document data provenance selectively.

description: Published benchmark results, leaderboards, and comparative evaluations — Open LLM Leaderboard, Chatbot Arena, and results publishing.
parity_rationale: Leaderboards are open but results are often self-reported. Independent evaluation infrastructure is underfunded.

description: Standardized model documentation — capabilities, limitations, intended use, training data, and ethical considerations.
parity_rationale: Model card tooling exists but quality varies wildly. Closed providers publish polished cards; many open models ship with minimal documentation.

description: Example outputs, interactive demos, and showcase applications that demonstrate model capabilities.
parity_rationale: Open source demos (Gradio, Streamlit, HF Spaces) are a unique strength. The demo ecosystem is overwhelmingly open.

description: License terms for source code — license scanning, compliance tooling, and open source license management.
parity_rationale: License scanning tools exist but AI-specific code licensing (training code, fine-tuning scripts) has unresolved questions.

description: License terms for training data — data licensing frameworks, consent documentation, and rights management.
parity_rationale: Open data licensing is more transparent than closed. CDLA, ODC, and CC frameworks are well-established.

description: Usage policies, acceptable use terms, and terms-of-service analysis tooling for AI products.
parity_rationale: Almost no open source tooling for ToS analysis or comparison. Closed providers set terms unilaterally.

description: License terms for model weights — Llama Community License, RAIL, OpenRAIL, and weight-specific licensing frameworks.
parity_rationale: Weight licensing is actively evolving. Open frameworks (RAIL, Llama license) exist but lack standardization.

description: How models are distributed and access-controlled — staged releases, gated downloads, and responsible disclosure practices.
parity_rationale: Closed providers have established release processes. Open model releases vary from careful (Llama) to permissive (community fine-tunes).

description: Third-party audits, transparency reports, bias assessments, and safety auditing infrastructure.
parity_rationale: Auditing tooling is sparse. Closed providers publish transparency reports; open models rarely undergo systematic safety audits.

description: Decision-making structures, oversight mechanisms, and AI governance tooling — policy frameworks and organizational governance.
parity_rationale: AI governance is mostly institutional, not software. Open governance tools are early-stage.

description: Content filtering, safety guardrails, toxicity detection, and content moderation systems.
parity_rationale: Open moderation tools (Llama Guard, Perspective API) exist but closed providers have more sophisticated multi-layered systems.

description: Techniques to align model behavior with human values — RLHF, constitutional AI, red teaming, and alignment research tooling.
parity_rationale: Alignment research is published openly but production alignment techniques (RLHF at scale, constitutional AI) are practiced primarily by closed labs.
